epithet: A shelter for the days of trial
lede: Four stories, and one question running under all of them: what do you hold on to when you are tested — in your faith, in your wealth, in what you know, in the power you are given? It is the surah the Prophet ﷺ set against the greatest trial of all.

names.name: al-Kahf
names.note: After the cave in which the young men took refuge with their faith (ayat 9–26). It is the name the Prophet ﷺ used: “Whoever memorises ten ayat from the beginning of Sūrat al-Kahf…” (Muslim 809).

names.name: Sūrat Aṣḥāb al-Kahf
names.note: A longer form of the same name, found in some reports and in the books of tafsir.

revelation.detail: Ibn al-Jawzī records it as Makkan from Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan, Mujāhid and Qatādah, and calls this the agreement of the commentators, without any difference he knew of. Two exceptions are reported and neither is the stronger view: that ayah 28 came down in Madinah, and — from Muqātil — that its opening as far as ayah 8, and ayat 107–108, did. Al-Qurṭubī mentions the claim about the opening and answers it in three words: the first view is sounder.

evidence.quote: رَوى أبُو صالِحٍ عَنِ ابْنِ عَبّاسٍ أنَّ سُورَةَ ( الكَهْفِ ) مَكِّيَّةٌ، وكَذَلِكَ قالَ الحَسَنُ، ومُجاهِدٌ، وقَتادَةُ. وهَذا إجْماعُ المُفَسِّرِينَ مِن غَيْرِ خِلافٍ نَعْلَمُهُ
وَهِيَ مَكِّيَّةٌ فِي قَوْلِ جَمِيعِ الْمُفَسِّرِينَ. رُوِيَ عَنْ فِرْقَةٍ أَنَّ أَوَّلَ السُّورَةِ نَزَلَ بِالْمَدِينَةِ إِلَى قَوْلِهِ: "جُرُزاً"، وَالْأَوَّلُ أَصَحُّ

attested.quote: أخْرَجَ النَّحّاسُ في ”ناسِخِهِ“، وابْنُ مَرْدُويَهْ، عَنِ اِبْنِ عَبّاسٍ قالَ: نَزَلَتْ سُورَةُ ”الكَهْفِ“ بِمَكَّةَ
attested.says: Ibn ʿAbbās: it came down in Makkah. Recorded by al-Naḥḥās and Ibn Mardawayh.

attested.quote: قالَ القُرْطُبِيُّ: وهي مَكِّيَّةٌ في قَوْلِ جَمِيعِ المُفَسِّرِينَ

setting: It came down in the later years in Makkah, when the argument had been running for a long time. Quraysh had run out of answers of their own: they could not call the Qurʾan poetry — they had poets, and it was not that; they could not call him a liar — they had named him the Trustworthy themselves. What they still had was power, and the believers were a small community under pressure, being asked to give up either its faith or its place in the city.

To such people the surah shows others who faced the same choice. Young men who left their city and took shelter in a cave, saying: “Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself, and provide for us right guidance in our affair.” A man with two gardens who forgot who had given them. Mūsā, a messenger of resolve, travelling to learn from a servant of Allah who had been taught what he had not. And a ruler given the means to everything, who reached the setting place of the sun and its rising, and said of his greatest work: “This is a mercy from my Lord.”

Four trials, then — of faith, of wealth, of knowledge and of power — and in the middle of them the one who stands behind every trial, refusing to bow (18:50). The Prophet ﷺ tied the surah to the last and greatest of them: whoever keeps ten ayat of its opening by heart, he said, will be protected from the Dajjāl.

Within the stories it sets a correction, gentle and permanent, about how a servant speaks of tomorrow: “Do not say of anything, ‘I shall do that tomorrow,’ without ‘if Allah wills’” (18:23). And it tells the Prophet ﷺ whose company to keep: “Keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His Face, and do not let your eyes pass beyond them” (18:28).

occasions.title: The nobles and the poor
occasions.text: The leading men of Quraysh asked the Prophet ﷺ to sit with them alone and to keep the poorer believers — Bilāl, ʿAmmār, Ṣuhayb, Khabbāb, Ibn Masʿūd — in a gathering of their own. He was told instead to keep himself patiently with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening. Saʿd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ describes the same demand in Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim (2413), concerning the sister ayah in al-Anʿām (6:52).
occasions.source: Ibn Kathīr, who introduces it with “it is said”. Al-Ṭabarī, al-Baghawī, Ibn al-Jawzī, al-Qurṭubī and al-Suyūṭī relate it too.

evidence.quote: يُقَالُ: إِنَّهَا نَزَلَتْ فِي أَشْرَافِ قُرَيْشٍ، حِينَ طَلَبُوا مِنَ النَّبِيِّ ﷺ أَنْ يَجْلِسَ مَعَهُمْ وَحْدَهُ وَلَا يُجَالِسَهُمْ بِضُعَفَاءِ أَصْحَابِهِ كَبِلَالٍ وَعَمَّارٍ وَصُهَيْبٍ

occasions.title: Mūsā and al-Khiḍr, as he ﷺ told it
occasions.text: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ tell what lay behind the journey. Mūsā stood up to address the Children of Israel and was asked: who is the most knowing of people? He said: “I am.” Allah reproved him, because he had not referred the knowledge back to Him, and revealed to him: “I have a servant at the meeting of the two seas who knows more than you.” Mūsā said: “My Lord, how can I reach him?” He was told to carry a fish in a basket: wherever he lost the fish, there the man would be.
story: He set out with his young attendant, Yūshaʿ ibn Nūn. At the rock they laid down their heads and slept. The fish stirred in the basket, slipped out of it and fell into the sea, and Allah held back the flow of the water from it, so that it stood over its path like an arch. When Mūsā woke, his companion forgot to tell him. They walked on for the rest of that day and through the night, and the next morning Mūsā said: “Bring us our meal; this journey of ours has wearied us” — and he had felt no weariness, the Prophet ﷺ said, until he had passed the place Allah had commanded. The young man remembered: at the rock he had forgotten the fish, and it had taken its way into the sea, a thing to wonder at. “That is what we were seeking,” said Mūsā, and they turned back, following their own footprints.

At the rock was a man wrapped in a garment. Mūsā greeted him, and al-Khiḍr said: “And how is there a greeting of peace in your land?” — “I am Mūsā.” — “Mūsā of the Children of Israel?” — “Yes. I have come to you so that you may teach me something of the right guidance you have been taught.” He said: “You will not be able to bear with me patiently. Mūsā, I have a knowledge from the knowledge of Allah which He has taught me and which you do not know; and you have a knowledge from the knowledge of Allah which He has taught you and which I do not know.” Mūsā promised patience, and al-Khiḍr set his condition: if you follow me, ask me about nothing until I speak of it to you myself.

They walked along the shore. A ship passed, and its people recognised al-Khiḍr and took them aboard without a fare. Before Mūsā knew it he had prised out one of the ship’s planks with an adze. “People who carried us for nothing — and you go to their ship and breach it, to drown those aboard?” — “Did I not say you would not be able to bear with me?” — “Do not hold me to what I forgot.” The first, said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, was forgetfulness on Mūsā’s part. Then a sparrow came and perched on the edge of the ship and dipped its beak once into the sea, and al-Khiḍr said to him: “My knowledge and your knowledge, beside the knowledge of Allah, are no more than what this sparrow has taken from the sea.”

They left the ship, and as they walked on the shore al-Khiḍr saw a boy playing with other boys, and killed him. “Have you killed an innocent soul, when he had killed no one?” — and this, he ﷺ said, was harder than the first. Mūsā said: “If I ask you about anything after this, keep me with you no longer.” They came to a town and asked its people for food, and were refused hospitality; and there they found a wall, leaning, about to fall, and al-Khiḍr set it straight with his hand. Mūsā said: “People we came to who would not feed us or take us in — had you wished, you could have taken a wage for it.” He said: “This is the parting between me and you,” and told him the meaning of the three things he had not been able to bear.
And the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: “We would have loved Mūsā to have been patient, so that Allah might have told us more of what passed between them.”
occasions.source: Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, through Ibn ʿAbbās: al-Bukhārī (4725) and Muslim (2380).

aim: To set out how a believer is to deal with trials, and to give living examples of it.

outline.title: A Book with no crookedness in it
outline.summary: Praise to Allah, who sent down the Book upon His servant and made it straight: a warning of a severe punishment, good news for the believers, and a warning to those who say that Allah has taken a son. The Prophet ﷺ is consoled — do not grieve yourself to death over them — and the key to the whole surah is given: everything on the earth is an adornment, set there to test which of them is best in deed.

outline.title: The Companions of the Cave
outline.summary: The first story, and the trial of faith. Young men who believed in their Lord when their people did not, and who left everything and took shelter in a cave with a single prayer (18:10). Allah made them sleep for three hundred years and nine, turned them from side to side, and woke them as a sign that His promise is true and the Hour is not in doubt. Inside the story, the lesson about “tomorrow” (18:23).

outline.title: Whose company to keep
outline.summary: Recite what has been revealed to you; no one changes His words. Keep yourself patient with those who call on their Lord morning and evening, and do not let your eyes pass beyond them to the glitter of this life. The truth is from your Lord: whoever wills may believe, and whoever wills may refuse — and then the Fire, and the Gardens.

outline.title: The man of the two gardens
outline.summary: The second story, and the trial of wealth. Two men, one of them given two gardens of vines and palms with a river between them. He walks into his garden wronging himself: “I do not think this will ever perish, and I do not think the Hour is coming.” His companion answers him with the words every believer has since been taught to say on seeing what pleases him (18:39). By morning the garden is fallen on its trellises.

outline.title: What this life is like
outline.summary: Rain, and a green that the wind scatters the next day. Wealth and children are the adornment of this life, and the lasting good deeds are better with your Lord. Then the day the mountains are moved, the people are stood in rows, and the record is laid open that leaves out nothing small or great.

outline.title: The enemy, and the excuse
outline.summary: Iblīs refused to bow to Ādam — will you then take him and his offspring as allies in place of Me? Every kind of example has been set out in this Qurʾan, and man is more given to argument than anything. Nothing kept them from believing except waiting for what befell those before them; and your Lord is the Forgiving, full of mercy — the towns were not destroyed until they had been given their term.

outline.title: Mūsā and al-Khiḍr
outline.summary: The third story, and the trial of knowledge. Mūsā, asked who was the most learned of men, had answered that he was; so he was sent to a servant of Allah who had been taught what he had not (al-Bukhārī 122, Muslim 2380). A boat is holed, a boy is killed, a wall is rebuilt for nothing — and three times Mūsā cannot be patient with what he has no knowledge of. Then each is explained, and behind each is a mercy that could not be seen from where he stood.

outline.title: Dhū al-Qarnayn
outline.summary: The fourth story, and the trial of power. A king who was given the means to everything and followed them to the setting of the sun, to its rising, and to a people between two mountains who begged him for a barrier against Yaʾjūj and Maʾjūj. He builds it of iron and molten copper, refuses their payment, and says what the owner of the garden never said: “This is a mercy from my Lord.”

outline.title: The greatest losers
outline.summary: The barrier will come down when the promise comes; the Trumpet is blown. “Shall We tell you who loses most in their deeds? Those whose effort is lost in this life while they think they are doing good.” For those who believe and do right, the Gardens of Firdaws. If the sea were ink for the words of my Lord it would run dry first. And the last ayah gathers the surah into one sentence: whoever hopes to meet his Lord, let him do righteous work, and associate no one in the worship of his Lord.

keyAyah.why: The prayer of the young men as they entered the cave. They ask for two things only, mercy and right guidance in their affair, and the rest of the surah shows what it looks like when those are given.

virtues.text: “Whoever memorises ten ayat from the beginning of Sūrat al-Kahf will be protected from the Dajjāl.” In another wording in Muslim: “from the end of al-Kahf.”
virtues.arabic: مَنْ حَفِظَ عَشْرَ آيَاتٍ مِنْ أَوَّلِ سُورَةِ الْكَهْفِ عُصِمَ مِنَ الدَّجَّالِ

virtues.text: In the long hadith of the Dajjāl: “Whoever among you lives to see him, let him recite over him the opening ayat of Sūrat al-Kahf.”

A man was reciting Sūrat al-Kahf with a horse tethered beside him, and a cloud came over him and drew nearer and nearer until the horse began to shy. In the morning he told the Prophet ﷺ, who said: “That was the tranquillity, descending for the Qurʾan.”
“Whoever recites Sūrat al-Kahf on the day of Friday, a light will shine for him between the two Fridays.”
virtues.caveat: This is al-Albānī’s grading as an index of his works records it; it has not yet been checked here against the printed book.

before: Al-Isrāʾ closes on praise — “All praise is for Allah, who has not taken a son” (17:111) — and al-Kahf opens on praise and warns those who say that He has (18:4). The three questions are answered across the pair: the spirit there (17:85), the young men and the traveller here.
after: Maryam carries on with wonders that only Allah’s power explains: a son to Zakariyyā in old age, and a son to Maryam with no father at all. And the saying that al-Kahf opened by condemning — that Allah has taken a son — is where Maryam ends (19:88).
